Asia Pacific Kite

GeometryTrianglesCircles
Game: Move a line through one corner of a four-sided shape to see the path of the point where two diagonals cross.
How to play: Drag E or F to turn the line, or drag A, B, C or D to change the shape. Focus a point and use the arrow keys, then press Check the claims to test what you see.
Look for the math

Here is a shape made by gluing two equilateral triangles along AC. Turn a line through D and watch the crossing point M. It looks free, but it is stuck on one circle.

A kite from two equilateral triangles

The four sides AB, BC, CD and DA are the same length, and the angle at B is 60°. So triangle ABC is equilateral, and so is triangle ACD. That makes AC = AB = BC = CD = DA. The diagonals AC and BD cross at right angles, and the long diagonal is BD = AC × √3. When you drag a corner, the opposite corner moves to keep these facts true.

The circle that M never leaves

Put E on the line AB past A and F on the line BC past C, as in the original problem. Let M be where CE and AF meet. Then M sits on the arc AC of the circumcircle of ABC, away from B, and the angle at M in triangle AMC is 120°. If you slide E past B instead, the angle is 60° and M runs along the other arc. Both arcs are the same circle. The logic test checks this at thousands of line positions; dragging E from one side of A to the other really does take M around the whole circle.

Why the two small circles just touch AC

The discussion on the old page gives CA² = CM × CE and CA² = AM × AF. Look at the circle through A, E and M: the line from C cuts it at M and E, so CM × CE is the power of C. That power equals CA², which is exactly the tangent length from C. So the circle touches AC at A. The same argument makes the circle through C, F and M touch AC at C.

The third point N is on the same line

The circles (AEM) and (CFM) already share M; call their other meeting point N. An angle chase with inscribed angles gives ∠MNE + ∠MNF = 180°. The two angles make a straight line, so E, N and F are in a row. Since the line through E and F also passes through D, N lies on that line too. The logic test finds N by intersecting the two circles and checks this for every position of the line.

Try dragging E just past A, then over toward B: watch M slide from the lower arc to the upper one and see the angle change from 120° to 60°.
